stationary-states.title: Stationary States
stationary-states.content:
Eigenstates of the self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator \( \hat{H} \) that possess definite energy eigenvalues \( E_n \) govern the time-independent behavior of quantum mechanical systems, providing the foundation for analyzing stable atomic configurations and spectroscopic transitions. These specific physical configurations represent states where all observables remain invariant in time, ensuring that the physical properties of the system are dynamically stable. In loop quantum gravity, the quantum spatial geometries are represented as discrete states in a Hilbert space spanned by Spin Networks, which determine the eigenvalues of spatial geometry and represent the stationary configurations of quantum gravity. In the quantum measurement problem, the transition between these deterministic states and the macroscopic observer is sometimes explained by Consciousness-Based Collapse, which postulates that conscious observation triggers a non-unitary transition, illustrating the debate surrounding wave-function collapse.

Relativistic formulations of these stationary quantum states require that the time evolution respects the causal structure of special relativity, ensuring that the coordinate transformations satisfy Poincaré invariance under the group \( P \). Within the flat four-dimensional manifold described by The Minkowski Metric \( \eta_{\mu u} \), the coordinates \( x^\mu \) and momentum components are coupled through the covariant wave equations, where the metric tensor is used to construct Lorentz invariant kinetic terms in the action with spacetime interval \( ds^2 = \eta_{\mu u} dx^\mu dx^ u \). The metric tensor \( \eta_{\mu u} \) determines the spacetime interval, establishing that the temporal phase of the stationary state transforms covariantly under Lorentz boosts, preventing unphysical reference frame choices from distorting the calculated probability density. By formulating the stationary states covariantly, the action principle guarantees that the physical energy eigenvalues are Lorentz invariant observables, ensuring that all observers measure identical spectral lines.

The mathematical representation of these stable configurations is obtained by solving the time-independent Schrödinger equation, where the wave functions must satisfy boundary conditions that represent physical state constraints. In this Hilbert space framework, the wave functions must satisfy the condition of Square-Integrability, which requires that the integral of the squared absolute value of the wave function over all space is finite, guaranteeing that the probability density can be normalized to unity. The time evolution of these states is generated by the Hamiltonian Operator \( \hat{H} \), whose action on the wave function yields the energy eigenvalues, proving that the energy is a conserved quantity. The wave function of these states is mathematically represented by the Stationary State Time-Evolution Relation:

\[ \Psi(x,t) = \psi_n(x) e^{- rac{i E_n t}{\hbar}} \]
In this expression, \( \Psi(x,t) \) is the complete time-dependent wave function, \( \psi_n(x) \) represents the spatial eigenfunction with quantum number \( n \), \( E_n \) is the energy eigenvalue, and \( \hbar \) is the reduced Planck constant. This relation mathematically guarantees that the temporal phase factor is a pure phase shift, proving that the probability density \( |\Psi(x,t)|^2 = |\psi_n(x)|^2 \) is completely independent of time, showing that the physical system remains in a stationary configuration along its dynamical evolution, preventing unphysical state decay.

The variational derivation of these eigenvalue equations is executed by applying the principles of analytical mechanics to the coupled wave fields, where the field dynamics is governed by a covariant density. In this field-theoretic framework, the field equations are derived by applying the variational principle to the action integral constructed from the Lagrangian density \( \mathcal{L}(\phi, \partial_\mu \phi) \) that couples the field variables \( \phi(x,t) \) and its derivatives in a Lorentz invariant manner, yielding eigenvalues \( \lambda \). The stationary states represent configurations where the action remains stationary under small variations of the field, establishing the link between classical analytical mechanics and the eigenvalue equations of quantum mechanics, demonstrating that the stationary states are the extremum configurations of the action.

The classical limiting case of these stationary quantum states is achieved in the macroscopic limit where the quantum number \( n o \infty \), a physical transition described by the Bohr correspondence principle, where the quantum wave functions \( \psi(x) \) contract onto the classical probability distributions \( P(x) \) of deterministic orbits. In this classical limit, the highly oscillatory quantum probability density contracts to the classical time-spent distribution of a classical particle moving along its trajectory, showing that quantum wave mechanics contracts to classical mechanics. This mathematical transition guarantees that the discrete energy eigenvalues contract into the continuous energy spectrum of classical mechanics without loss of consistency, demonstrating that classical orbits are the high-energy limit of a deeper quantum mechanical framework, completing the classical transition.

ehrenfests-theorem.title: Ehrenfest's Theorem
ehrenfests-theorem.content:
Expectation values of quantum mechanical operators \( \hat{X}_i \) and \( \hat{P}_i \) satisfy dynamical equations of motion that directly parallel the canonical equations of classical mechanics, providing the foundational bridge between wave mechanics and deterministic trajectories. This physical correspondence guarantees that the quantum wave packet behaves as a classical particle on average, illustrating how the laws of classical mechanics emerge from the underlying quantum probability distributions and coordinate variables \( q_i \). In alternative formulations of quantum mechanics, such as Objective Collapse Models, the deterministic Schrödinger evolution is modified by stochastic terms that trigger a physical collapse of the wavefunction, preventing macroscopic superpositions without relying on observers. The spatial profile of the physical state is characterized by a localized Wave Packet \( \psi(x,t) \), whose spatial dispersion determines the uncertainty in coordinate and momentum measurements, showing how quantum spread influences the transition to classical dynamics.

Relativistic formulations of these expectation relations require that the coordinate operators and momentum operator components respect the causal structure of special relativity, ensuring that the observer-dependent expectation values transform covariantly under Lorentz boosts. Within the flat four-dimensional spacetime described by The Minkowski Metric \( \eta_{\mu\nu} \), the coordinates \( x^\mu \) and derivative operators are coupled using the metric tensor to construct Lorentz invariant wave equations, establishing the relativistic framework for quantum expectation values. The metric tensor \( \eta_{\mu\nu} \) determines the relativistic kinematics, establishing that the four-momentum expectation value \( \langle p^\mu \rangle \) transforms covariantly as a four-vector under Lorentz boosts, preventing unphysical reference frame choices from distorting the calculated trajectories. By formulating the expectation relations covariantly, the action principle guarantees that the physical equations of motion preserve their mathematical form for all observers moving at constant velocities.

The derivation of these expectation equations is executed by calculating the commutator of the operators with the Hamiltonian, which generates the time evolution in the Heisenberg picture. In the variational formulation of the wave dynamics, the field equations can be derived from a covariant action constructed from the Lagrangian density \( \mathcal{L}(\phi, \partial_\mu \phi) \), which couples the fields and their derivatives in a Poincaré invariant manner. The time evolution of the momentum expectation value is mathematically governed by the Ehrenfest Momentum Expectation Relation:

\\[ \frac{d}{dt}\langle p_i \rangle = -\left\langle \frac{\partial V}{\partial x_i} \right\rangle \\]
In this expression, \( \langle p_i \rangle \) is the expectation value of the momentum operator, \( V(x_i) \) represents the classical potential energy, and \( \langle \partial V / \partial x_i \rangle \) is the expectation value of the gradient of the potential, which represents the quantum force operator. This relation mathematically guarantees that the quantum expectation values obey Newton's second law on average, showing how classical dynamics is recovered from the average behavior of wave functions, ensuring that classical mechanical concepts are preserved at the operator level.

The classical limit of these expectation relations is closely connected to the wave-front mechanics of classical systems, where the action principal function determines the trajectories. This classical wave-front propagation is governed by The Hamilton-Jacobi Equation, which describes how the wave-fronts of constant action propagate through the configuration space, establishing the link between classical mechanics and the Schrödinger equation under quantum phase \( \theta = S/\hbar \). The correspondence between the expectation relations and classical wave-fronts illustrates how the quantum phase \( S \) matches the classical action, showing that the wave packet center-of-mass moves along the paths perpendicular to the constant phase fronts, providing the mechanical foundation for the classical recovery.

In relativistic quantum field theories, the expectation values of fields are analyzed using the formalism of green's functions and correlation functions, which govern the scattering amplitudes. The calculation of these vacuum expectation values of field operators \( \phi(x) \) is executed using the algebraic rules of Correlation Functions and Wick's Theorem, which reduces the time-ordered products of field operators to sum of contractions, providing the foundation for Feynman diagrammatic expansion and n-point correlation functions \( \langle 0 | T \phi(x_1) \dots \phi(x_n) | 0 \rangle \). The study of correlation functions illustrates how the field expectation values satisfy relativistic equations that generalize the single-particle expectation relations, showing how the multi-particle dynamics is constrained by the underlying field equations.

The macroscopic limiting case of these expectation relations is achieved as Planck's constant \( \hbar \to 0 \) and the spatial width of the wave packet vanishes, causing the expectation value of the force operator to contract into the force evaluated at the expectation value of the position, \( \langle F(x) \rangle \to F(\langle x \rangle) \). In this classical limit, the quantum uncertainty vanishes, and the coupled expectation relations contract into the deterministic Newton's equations of classical mechanics, \( dp_i / dt = -\partial V / \partial x_i \), where the coordinates and momenta are measured simultaneously without uncertainty. This mathematical transition guarantees that classical mechanics is recovered without loss of consistency, demonstrating that classical deterministic orbits are the low-energy limit of a deeper quantum mechanical framework, completing the classical transition.

energy-eigenvalues.title: Energy Eigenvalues
energy-eigenvalues.content:
Spectral components of the self-adjoint Hamiltonian operator \( \hat{H} \) define the allowed energy levels of a physical system, establishing the fundamental algebraic constraints that govern quantum mechanical dynamics. This mathematical spectrum dictates the frequencies of emitted and absorbed radiation during state transitions, providing the foundation for all quantum mechanical calculations and spectroscopic observations. Within the rigorous framework of quantum mechanics, these states are represented as vectors in Hilbert Space \( \mathcal{H} \), where the operators must satisfy self-adjoint conditions to ensure that their eigenvalues \( E_n \) are real numbers. To analyze the phase-space behavior of these states, physicists employ The Wigner Quasi-Probability Distribution \( W(q,p) \), which provides a semiclassical representation of the quantum state in phase space, showing how quantum states are distributed over the classical coordinates and momenta.

Relativistic formulations of these energy spectrum equations require that the Hamiltonian operator and its eigenvalues are defined in a manner that respects the causal structure of spacetime. Within the flat four-dimensional manifold described by The Minkowski Metric \( \eta_{\mu\nu} \), the coordinates \( x^\mu \) and derivative operators are coupled through the covariant wave equations, where the mass-shell constraint determines the energy spectrum under Lorentz boosts of the group \( SO(1,3) \). The metric tensor \( \eta_{\mu\nu} \) determines the spacetime interval, establishing that the energy eigenvalues transform covariantly as the temporal component of the four-momentum vector under Lorentz boosts, preventing unphysical reference frame choices from distorting the calculated spectrum. By defining the energy operator covariantly, the action principle guarantees that the physical energy eigenvalues are Lorentz invariant observables, ensuring that all observers measure identical spectral lines.

The variational derivation of these eigenvalue equations is executed by applying the principles of analytical mechanics to the coupled wave fields, where the field dynamics is governed by a covariant density. In this field-theoretic framework, the field equations are derived by applying the variational principle to the Action Integral \( S = \int \mathcal{L} \, d^4x \) constructed from the Lagrangian density \( \mathcal{L} \) that couples the field variables \( \phi(x) \) and their derivatives in a Lorentz invariant manner. The energy eigenvalues represent configurations where the action remains stationary under small variations of the fields, establishing the link between classical analytical mechanics and the eigenvalue equations of quantum mechanics.

The equations of motion that govern the field dynamics are derived by applying the Euler-Lagrange equations to the action density, ensuring that the field propagation respects the conservation laws of the theory. In this classical framework, the field equations correspond to the Euler-Lagrange Equations for the continuous fields \( \phi_a(x) \) that relate the field variables and their spacetime derivatives, proving that the energy eigenvalues \( E_a \) are conserved quantities. The eigenvalue equations represent the stationary solutions to these field equations, showing how the continuous classical fields are quantized into discrete energy states when subject to localized boundary conditions.

The mathematical structure of the state space is characterized by a countable basis of wave functions, ensuring that the physical observables can be diagonalized using standard operator techniques. In this rigorous framework, the state space is restricted to Separable Hilbert Spaces \( \mathcal{H}_s \), which possess a countable dense subset and allow the definition of a complete orthonormal basis of energy eigenfunctions \( \psi_n \) represented by basis vectors \( |n\rangle \). This separable structure guarantees that the Hamiltonian operator can be diagonalized to yield a countable set of eigenvalues, showing how the physical state space is constructed from a countable set of wave functions, ensuring that the physical predictions remain mathematically consistent.

The classical limiting case of these energy spectrum equations is achieved in the macroscopic limit where Planck's constant \( \hbar \to 0 \) and the quantum number \( n \to \infty \), causing the discrete eigenvalues to contract into the continuous energy spectrum of classical mechanics. In this classical limit, the highly oscillatory wave functions contract onto the deterministic classical trajectories, and the energy eigenvalue equation contracts into the classical Hamilton-Jacobi equation. The eigenvalue relation is mathematically governed by the Hamiltonian Energy Eigenvalue Equation:

\\[ \hat{H} \psi_n = E_n \psi_n \\]
In this expression, \( \hat{H} \) is the Hamiltonian operator, \( \psi_n \) represents the energy eigenfunction with quantum number \( n \), and \( E_n \) is the associated energy eigenvalue. This relation mathematically guarantees that the allowed energy states of the system are quantized, showing how quantum mechanics contains classical mechanics as a low-energy, deterministic limit, completing the classical transition.
